title: The Grumpy Cactus and the Lost City
markdown:
The desert had a sense of humour. Ari Cohen knew it the way he knew the back of his own sun-worn hand. His eyes, the colour of the clearest sky, had seen more dawns over endless dunes than most folk see in a lifetime. He moved with quiet grace, a silent conversation between man and miles of golden sand.

Then came Lord Pembroke, whose boundless, if misguided, archaeological enthusiasm knew no bounds. He arrived not on a sturdy camel but in a sputtering motorcar, a wheezing contraption utterly out of place, like a peacock at a camel auction. And with him, yapping from a velvet cushion, was Bartholomew, a terrier so small it looked like a fluffy, opinionated dust bunny with serious zoomies.

“My dear Cohen,” Lord Pembroke boomed, adjusting his pith helmet. “The legends speak of Zoltharr. A civilisation lost to the ages, buried beneath these sands. I have deciphered the ancient scrolls — a postcard from a bazaar, I believe to be a primary source.”

Ari simply nodded, a faint smile playing on his lips, a small eddy in the vast calm of his patience. He had heard many tales of Zoltharr. Mostly from the wind, carrying whispers of forgotten journeys.

“The scrolls,” Pembroke continued, consulting a crumpled piece of parchment suspiciously like a diner menu, “clearly indicate a path requiring seven left turns, three U-turns, and a detour around a grumpy cactus. The cartography is incredibly sophisticated.”

Ari blinked, the desert sun glinting. “Lord Pembroke, sir,” he began gently, his voice a low rumble. “The desert doesn’t often conform to straight lines. It has its own rhythm.”

“Nonsense,” Pembroke declared, puffing out his chest, Bartholomew yapping in agreement. “The ancient Zoltharrans were masters of geometry. Cities of impossible precision. This way.” He pointed dramatically towards a shimmering dip in the sand. A place Ari knew well.

Meanwhile the local camel herders, lounging under an acacia, watched with twinkling eyes. They knew these foreigners. Always thinking they knew better than the sand, the wind, and the sun. To them, Pembroke was just a particularly entertaining character.

They set off, Bartholomew’s frantic yaps echoing. After an eternity of U-turns and squealing cactus avoidance, they found themselves not at a lost city’s gates, but beside a surprisingly lush oasis. Palm trees swayed. A clear pool shimmered. The air was thick with the sweet scent of blossoms. Beautiful, but hardly a metropolis.

“Eureka,” Lord Pembroke shrieked, leaping from his motorcar, scattering Bartholomew and several startled desert mice. “The Sunken City. Behold, its magnificent central plaza.” He gestured wildly at a sandy clearing with scattered stones.

Ari surveyed the scene. The plaza looked like a well-worn gathering spot. The carvings on a nearby rock, which Pembroke was already inspecting with a magnifying glass, seemed less like forgotten runes and more like helpful directions.

“That symbol,” Ari said, pointing to a stone, “means fresh water this way. Universal language. This one,” he indicated another, “usually means beware of delicious dates, and don’t try to carry too many.”

Pembroke squinted, Bartholomew panting on his cushion, a furry witness to his owner’s grand delusion. “Dates? But the scrolls said… ah, yes. Succulent fruit appearing at the zenith of their civilisation. It’s all falling into place.”

As Pembroke rallied for a grand pronouncement, villagers emerged from behind the palms, their faces etched with warm smiles. They carried baskets laden with dates, figs, and water skins.

An elder, her face a roadmap of wisdom, approached. She spoke in a language of gentle clicks and warm inflections, a melody of the desert.

“Lord Pembroke,” Ari translated, his voice calm, “she says this is not Zoltharr. This is Omar’s Rest, a convenient watering hole. The carvings are helpful signs left by generations. The sacred artefacts are simply useful pottery shards for scooping water. And yes,” he added with a slight smile, “the dates are indeed succulent.”

Lord Pembroke stood frozen, his pith helmet tilting further. Bartholomew, sensing the shift, curled into a tiny, embarrassed ball.

“But the discovery,” Pembroke stammered, his voice a whisper. “The grandeur. The lost civilisation.”

The elder chuckled, a sound like dry leaves rustling. She offered Pembroke a plump date. He took it. He ate it. The pith helmet stayed crooked.

And so, with a bag full of delicious dates and a considerably less inflated ego, Lord Pembroke and his silent terrier departed. The desert kept its secrets, and its humour. Ari watched the motorcar wheeze back the way it had come, seven left turns none the wiser, and the oasis, which had never been lost, went on being exactly what it was.
characters: Ari Cohen (desert guide), Lord Pembroke (amateur archaeologist)
